title: IB Bonus Points: How TOK and EE Grades Combine
summary: IB bonus points explained: see how TOK and EE grades combine, use the core points matrix, and understand grade boundaries and diploma passing requirements.
body_markdown:
IB bonus points come from combining your Theory of Knowledge (TOK) and Extended Essay (EE) grades in the IB core points matrix. Together, they add **0-3 points** to your six subject grades, taking the maximum diploma score from 42 to 45. TOK and EE each receive a letter grade from A to E. An E in either is a failing condition for the diploma, regardless of your subject total.


The calculation becomes easier once you separate two questions: what grade did each piece of work receive, and how many points does that combination earn?


Imagine a student, Maya, reviewing a **hypothetical May 2026 results sheet** . Her six subjects total 34 points. Her TOK grade is B and her EE grade is C. She wonders whether the letters need converting into numbers and averaging. They do not. The matrix gives B/C two core points, bringing her total to **36 out of 45** .


### IB bonus points at a glance


Keep these rules beside your results:


- Six subjects contribute up to 42 points, with each graded from 1 to 7.
- TOK and EE together contribute up to three additional points.
- Their letter grades are combined using a matrix, rather than added or averaged.
- CAS is required for the diploma but contributes no points.
- A total of 24 points is the minimum for the diploma, and other passing conditions also apply.


For the wider scoring picture, RevisionDojo’s guide to[how IB grades work](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-is-ib-graded) explains the relationship between subject grades and the 45-point total.


### How the TOK and EE points matrix works


Find your TOK grade down the left and your EE grade across the top. The intersection shows your core points.


TOK grade / EE grade A B C D E


A 3 3 2 2 Failing condition


B 3 2 2 1 Failing condition


C 2 2 1 0 Failing condition


D 2 1 0 0 Failing condition


E Failing condition Failing condition Failing condition Failing condition Failing condition


**Three points require A/A, A/B, or B/A.** Two Bs earn two points. Two Cs earn one.


The matrix also explains a less obvious result: an A paired with a D earns two points, while a B paired with a D earns one. Improving a letter grade can therefore change the total differently depending on the other component.


Maya’s B/C combination earns two points. If her EE improved to B while TOK stayed at B, she would still receive two. If her TOK improved to A while the EE stayed at C, she would also remain on two. To reach three, she would need an A alongside an A or B.


That is why checking the matrix matters before setting a target. RevisionDojo’s explanation of[how TOK and EE affect your final score](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/tok-ee-points-ib-score) offers another way to work through these combinations.


A student suggests using a matrix while a parent brings an oversized calculator with letter buttons.


### Where IB grade boundaries enter the calculation


Maya now understands her total, but another question remains: how did her work become a B or C?


There are two separate conversion steps:


- **Assessment marks become grades.** The relevant IB grade boundaries determine the letter grade for TOK or EE.
- **Letter grades become core points.** The matrix converts those two grades into 0-3 points.


A boundary is a mark threshold. The matrix is a combination rule. Mixing them up can lead students to assume that an extra assessment mark automatically creates an extra diploma point.


It may make no difference to the letter grade. Even when it moves a grade up, the matrix may award the same number of core points.


Use boundaries for the relevant examination session and assessment version. Historical thresholds help you interpret practice marks, but they cannot guarantee a future result. Parents can find a fuller explanation in[RevisionDojo’s guide to IB grade boundaries](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-grade-boundaries-explained-parent-guide) .


### Why “bonus” does not mean optional


The word “bonus” can make TOK and EE sound like extra credit. Both are required parts of the Diploma Programme core.


An E in either is a failing condition. A D is different: it does not itself trigger that condition, although some combinations involving D earn zero core points.


For a second **hypothetical May 2026 illustration** , consider a student with 30 subject points and D/D in the core. The matrix adds zero, leaving 30 points. Diploma eligibility still depends on meeting all the other requirements, including CAS and the subject-grade conditions.


Now consider a student with 38 subject points and an E in the EE. The strong subject total does not override the failing condition.


The practical lesson is to secure acceptable work in both components before chasing the final extra point. The[TOK minimum-grade guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/minimum-grade-to-pass-tok) explains the distinction between D and E in more detail.


### Turn your target into a useful study decision


Maya’s next decision is about effort. She has limited time, an EE draft to improve, and six subjects competing for attention.


A sensible approach starts with the assessment criteria. Identify where the work falls short, then ask what revision would address that weakness. A clearer research question or stronger evaluation is a more useful objective than simply writing “get an A” on a planner.


For TOK, review how effectively the argument answers the prescribed title and examines different perspectives. For the EE, check whether the research question, evidence, analysis, and conclusion support one another. Follow the guidance for your assessment cohort and discuss uncertainties with your teacher or supervisor.


RevisionDojo brings the wider preparation together. Study Notes and AI Chat can help clarify ideas; the Coursework Library can support discussion of structure and criteria. Grading tools can provide another perspective on a draft, with teacher guidance remaining central. Tutors can help students address persistent difficulties.


Meanwhile, the Questionbank, Flashcards, Mock Exams, and Predicted Papers support preparation across the six subjects. That balance matters: the core offers up to three points, while subjects account for up to 42.


### Give every point a clear meaning


Maya’s results sheet now tells a simpler story: 34 subject points, two core points, 36 overall. She can explain both the total and the limits of what it says about diploma eligibility.


Start with your two letter grades, check the matrix, and then review the full passing requirements.
